implementation_notes: mockall generates the double with a procedural macro: #[automock] on a trait (or mock! for what automock cannot express) produces MockTrait, the test programmes each expectation as mock.expect_method().with(predicate::eq(4)).times(1).returning(|x| x + 1), and any call outside the expectation panics so the failure points at the deviating call. Sequence and .in_sequence express ordering, checkpoint() performs an explicit final verification, and hand-written trait doubles remain the idiomatic fallback for a single canned answer because Rust traits make substitution trivial without a macro.
pitfalls: Expectations are verified when the mock is dropped, so a leaked mock or one kept alive past the test skips the check; call checkpoint() when verification must be explicit.
Mock objects are Send unless the non-Send helpers are used, so expectations capturing Rc or other non-Send values need the _st variants or the test will not compile.
Automock cannot mock every trait shape (generic methods, some lifetimes); fall back to mock! or a hand-written double rather than bending the API to fit the macro.
